extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and educated readers interested in architectural theory and ornamentation
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles for building design and ornament: how to arrange superimposed masses (shafts, walls, stories, towers, staircases) and what subjects/materials and treatments are appropriate for architectural decoration. Emphases on structural expression, honesty of construction, and the proper selection and subordination of ornamental subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of shafts to wall height
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion to the height of wall above them, the shafts are to be short. You may take your given height of wall, and turn any quantity of that wall into shaft that you like; but you must not turn it all into tall shafts, and then put more wall above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you add to the shaft you must take from the wall; shorter shafts should be proportionately (if not actually) thicker. (Example: in the Ducal Palace the shortest shafts are always the thickest.) This rule preserves visual stability when weight is superimposed on light supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superimposition: upper stories lighter and richer
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper stories shall be at once lighter and richer than the lower ones when arranging lightness on weight (stories one upon another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The value of such buildings depends on the perfect and easy expression of the relative strength of the stories, and the unity obtained by varieties of their proportions, while still frankly telling the fact of superimposition and separation by floors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of continuous shafts in buildings without floors
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no separation by floors, either frankly complete each story's archwork and cornice (honest/nobler way), or else tie stories by supplementary shafts from floor to roof (Northern Gothic practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tying shafts in a way that gives a scaffolding appearance with cross-poles; best method is to avoid any chance of shafts being supposed continuous by increasing their number and changing their places in upper stories so the work 'branches from the ground like a tree' (Byzantine/Pisan practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tower expression: diminishing weight on massy foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The true expression of the best and strongest towers is the elevation of gradually diminishing weight on a massy or solid foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Towers should only diminish weight upwards as necessary for balanced strength — no 'light-headedness.' They should serve their original purposes (defence, watch, landmark) with appropriate solidity rather than filigree ornament. Prefer massy cornices and battlements to delicate pinnacles or confectionery Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Towers must appear self-supporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Towers shall seem to stand, and shall verily stand, in their own strength; not by help of buttresses nor artful balancings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buttresses or angle projections, if present, must be integrated parts of the tower (like satellites to a shaft). When such supports lose unity with the main body and become true buttress walls, the tower loses dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation and increasing apertures toward summit
rubrics_metrics.description: A noble tower should show continual variation in arrangement of stories and a larger number of apertures towards the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplified in Lombardic towers: regular increase of window counts toward summit (e.g., one, then two, then three, five, six). Violations of this law produce modern towers that feel incoherent and purposeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concealed or inadequate visible support
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive architecture without visible or sufficient support is painful and unen durable; concealed ironwork or minimal rods beneath heavy walls make the eye unsatisfied as to security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When structural ironwork is concealed or insufficient relative to the mass above (e.g., fifty or sixty feet of wall above a narrow iron rod), the result is an appearance of impending failure; honesty of structural expression is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staircase as architectural feature: support and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern straight unsupported staircases are usually ugly and appear without support; medieval spiral staircases enclosed in an exterior tower, supported by bold shafts and arches, are superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-supported, externally-sited spiral stair adds picturesque effect and practical space-saving. Unsupported modern geometric staircases create awkward divisions in passages and windows and an impression of instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step process for decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: To decorate architecture: (1) find out what we like best in the world; (2) put as much of this as possible into form; (3) put the formed abstraction into a proper place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These successive inquiries correspond to: right material of ornament, right treatment, and right place. The author intends to discuss material (this chapter), treatment (next chapter), and placement (following discussion of architectural parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ornament that expresses delight in nature ('God's work')
rubrics_metrics.description: All noble ornamentation is the expression of man's delight in God's work; avoid ornament that is merely imitation of man's work (degraded classic/Renaissance tendency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author counsels to 'get rid of all this imitation of man's' work before inquiring what we like best of God's work. If one prefers man-made motifs, that's a matter of taste, but the prescriptive stance condemns such imitation as base or degraded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable categories of ornament derived from man's work (and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects of ornament from man's work fall into four heads: (1) instruments of art/agriculture/war (armor, dress), (2) drapery, (3) shipping, (4) architecture itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category may be appropriate in specific, subordinate, or symbolic contexts, but overuse or literal reproduction (especially when lifeless or 'cast' rather than living) is condemned. Use must respect the object's living or symbolic relation to the figure or building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armor/instruments as ornament: subordinate and living
rubrics_metrics.description: Armor is noble in its proper service and subordination to the body; a heap of cast skins or shed armor is unworthy of imitation. Renaissance over-emphasis on detailed, 'stage' armor is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptors should subordinate armor to principal figures (draped or naked) rather than making armor the focus; avoid lifeless shell-like depictions (a shield without a handle) and piles of costume as decorative filler (e.g., boots on Column Vendome). Instruments may be right when symbolic or informational but not as mere decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drapery as ornament: usually an error
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing drapery as such for ornament is an error; carved curtains and upholstery in stone are coarse and senseless vulgarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptionally, carved curtains in tomb sculpture (angels withdrawing curtains to reveal the dead) can be emotionally effective when lightly and tenderly handled, but when caricatured into huge marble tents with poles, the idea degrades and becomes vulgar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipping as sculpture subject: subordinate and schematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Though ships are among the loveliest human-made things, ships cannot be made prominent subjects of sculpture without destroying the sculpture; they may be used only in severe subordination as light background indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce maritime elements only sketched in the lightest lines on the background; never attempt full realization equal to the power of figures unless the whole subject is pictorial. The cable as an abstract twisted-line motif is acceptable; literal, detailed cables or ships in stone are curiosities, not admirations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture used as ornament: keep it subordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: The false use of architecture itself as ornament is conspicuous and grievous; in bas-relief architecture may be introduced as explanation of the scene but with prominence inverse to the importance of the figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where figures are of great value and beauty, it is impertinent to disturb contemplation with minor architectural features. If figures are life-size statues, carving a temple above them is gross vulgarity. For bas-relief, explain scenes with lightly traced architectural outlines (e.g., Ninevite marbles) rather than competing structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty vs. scaffold-like appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: When tying stories or structural elements together, avoid arrangements that suggest scaffolding or temporary supports; the 'honester' method is to complete each story and begin a new one above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If continuous slender shafts are necessary for economy, arrange them to avoid the illusion of continuous uprights by varying placement and number, so the composition branches naturally and avoids the look of tied scaffolding (Northern Gothic risk).
